name: a16z Crypto
title: RT by @a16zcrypto: A few reflections on the lattice vs. hash-only debate that our recent Aerie post sparked: 1. Cryptographic ossification for blockchains was never safe. Until the day we know with certainty that P ≠ NP, that finding short vectors in lattices is intractable, that Keccak effectively behaves like a random oracle in deployed SNARKs, and that every single bug has been eliminated from our codebases, blockchains cannot ossify. That is simply not how safe systems are built. Issues will arise, and the system will have to respond. It’s a double standard to reject lattices because blockchains are hard to upgrade if lattices break, while counting on upgrades if AI breaks your hash function or finds a critical zkVM bug. The best counterargument is that hash-only designs are more agile: if your hash function breaks, just swap out the hash. But we must aspire to a higher level of agility than this. Indeed, as I cover next, if SNARK recursion itself turns out to degrade security, the proposed hash-only blockchain designs would need to be rethought from the ground up. 2. The real security debate is not lattices vs. hashes — it is lattices vs. building everything on SNARK recursion. That’s because “hash-only” is not really hash-only: it rests on hashes plus the soundness of deep SNARK recursion. Ethereum’s roadmap relies on exactly that: hash-based aggregation needs recursion to keep up with a slot’s worth of signatures, and EIP-8288 would send other signature schemes and users’ own proofs through the same recursive pipeline. In contrast, Aerie proves a slot’s worth of signatures on one laptop without any recursion. All deployed post-quantum SNARKs rely on the Random Oracle Methodology (via Fiat–Shamir) to establish their security. This is an idealization we know fails in the real world: we have explicit counterexamples where “SNARKs” coming out of this methodology are totally insecure when instantiated with any concrete hash function. We generally ignore these counterexamples in part because they only arise when proving contrived, self-referential statements about the very hash function used by the SNARK verifier. But proving statements about the verifier’s own hash function is the exact thing you do in SNARK recursion. That’s why the security of recursive SNARKs can’t be established even in the random oracle model. On top of that, the standard security proofs for recursion (in other models) suffer an “extractor runtime” blowup that is exponential in the recursion depth, suggesting that security may degrade as more recursion is applied. Yet Ethereum’s own EIP-8288 enables unlimited-depth recursion, even as it lists soundness of recursive SNARKs as a trust assumption. Proofs in more idealized models avoid the blowup, but they mainly tell us that an attack on SNARK recursion would have to exploit the concrete hash function, which is exactly what the Fiat–Shamir attacks above do. To be clear, we don’t know of any outright attacks on SNARK recursion, and I very much hope it is secure. But some of us who have studied the question have a lingering sense that an attack may be possible in some settings. And if AI is going to supercharge cryptanalysis, there is no reason to expect it to spare Fiat–Shamir for SNARKs, let alone SNARK recursion, both of which have had far less scrutiny than lattices. So, I do not concede that a “recursion everywhere” hash-only approach is clearly more conservative than one built on standard lattice assumptions. 3. “Just wrap everything in a hash-based SNARK” (like EIP-8288) faces challenges. Aggregating signatures and proofs off-chain into a single block-level proof is a powerful design independent of the hash-only vs. lattice debate, and I am not telling people to avoid it. But claiming, as Vitalik Buterin did this week, that users can run whatever cryptography they want locally and wrap it in a client-side leanVM proof glosses over major hurdles. For example, leanVM today is a minimal VM designed almost entirely to prove hash-based signatures and recursion, not general-purpose computation. And binary-field SNARKs like leanVM remain slow at proving the integer multiplications that lattice cryptography does en masse. I am optimistic that many of these zkVM challenges can be met (including via my own work, binary-field Twist and Shout, which are now implemented in Magnetar). But regardless, if lattices can make aggregation simpler and faster, then they should be leveraged. We need to be agile no matter what. 4. For chains whose reason for existence is privacy, I truly struggle to understand the pushback. Public-key encryption (and fast single-server PIR) cannot be built from hashes alone, at least not in any black-box way. If lattices break, it is going to be very, very hard for these chains to provide acceptable levels of privacy and functionality. For a project whose entire reason for existence is privacy, a loss of confidentiality is an existential failure. Next to that, a second signature upgrade (after the first one, from elliptic curves alone to, hopefully, a hybrid lattice scheme) is easy. Summary: We don’t know for sure what is secure and what isn’t. We are all weighing unquantifiable risks against each other, and we do not need to agree on a total order on them. But hash-only solutions face many open engineering challenges, and they are not more “conservative” in the way some have argued. Some of those challenges are entirely prosaic and have nothing to do with bugs or cryptography, like hardware support for custom schemes whose hash function is still undecided. I hope we can overcome those challenges within the appropriate timelines, but they must be acknowledged and portrayed realistically. Overall, cryptographic agility and defense in depth (e.g., hybrid signatures) are the answer, which is why we are building both lattice-Jolt and hash-Jolt. In practice, the positions are less polarized than social media discourse suggests: for example, StarkWare is working to make Falcon verification cheap (https://falcon.provably.fast/), which is great to see. Here is the (apparently) controversial take I am sticking to: Conditioned on agility, whenever lattices make systems simpler or more functional, we should embrace them rather than default to “hash-only” designs. Lattices are what the rest of the world will depend on, with decades of study and hardening behind them, and at the system level, less functional often means less secure. Where hash-only designs are just as simple and functional, by all means use them.

This gives builders far more freedom to design incentives for different use cases across Bittensor.

name: Opentensor Foundation
title: R to @opentensor: Root TAO stakers receive part of each subnet's validator rewards. Cutting that allocation would normally reduce their share. To prevent this, eTAO automatically adjusts the subnet's effective TAO weight when the owner changes the split. Root stakers still receive the same share they would get under the default split. For example, if the validator share falls from 41% to 20%, the effective TAO weight can rise from 18% to 43.9%. Root still receives about 5.4% of the subnet's emissions.

name: Opentensor Foundation
title: R to @opentensor: Subnet owners can now adjust those percentages themselves. The protocol sets the following limits: > Owner: 0–33% (at least 18% for lease-created subnets) > Validators: up to 50%, with a variable minimum to protect root > Miners: at least 33% > Change frequency: owners can update the split roughly once every 7 days For example, an owner can keep 18%, allocate 20% to validators, and increase the miners' share to 62%.

name: Manako
title: Pinned: Most AI still automates tasks. The next shift is AI that can run business operations. The progression looks a lot like autonomous driving. Just as cars moved from driver assistance to partial, conditional, and higher autonomy, business operations will move through the same stages: 0. Manual operations → people observe, decide and act. 1. Assisted operations → AI detects events. People act. (This is where Vision Agents sit today.) 2. Partial automation → AI executes tasks. People supervise. 3. Conditional autonomy → AI runs workflows. People handle exceptions. 4. High autonomy → AI runs a defined operation, including its exceptions. 5. Autonomous operations — AI coordinates and improves end-to-end operations. The long-term direction is clear: increasing operational autonomy. People set the goals, the policies and the accountability. AI runs more of the operations. Humans govern. At Manako Labs, we’re building World Models for Business so this progression can actually happen in the physical world, starting with the cameras companies already have. Vision Agents are the entry point. Levels 2–5 are the ambition.

title: RT by @nigescore: Astra Ultra did not cook sports-grade vision AI. Gave it a 30s football clip from our subnet private track. Frame-level events, JSON, annotated video. Ground truth and the published scoring rules only after it committed. 22 predictions. 17 real events. 15 inside the action windows. 7 extras. 2 misses. Precision 68.18%. Recall 88.24%. F1 76.92%. Our Bittensor eval, SN44: 0%. Matches after timing decay: 16.538 False positives: −20.300 GT weight: 25.600 score = max(0, (16.538 − 20.300) / 25.600) = 0 Three extra take-ons and two extra tackles were 14.6 penalty points. It also misread the late interception/clearance. Rare actions pay more when you hit them and tax you harder when you invent them. Perfect timestamps on the matches still would not have cleared that bill. This was one offline replay of the published scorer. Unchanged preds. Not live latency. Not a season. The point is simpler than the arithmetic. F1 is what you post. SN44 is what you get paid on. Real matches, messy cameras, hard negatives, and a 30-second clock are not the same sport as a nice 15s clip to aura farm on Twitter.

name: Rob Greer
title: RT by @rob_svrn: Really interesting convo below from this weeks all in on why a16z stays away from the neoclouds, and it made something click for me about Bittensor. @bhorowitz point is that scaling compute on debt is a dangerous arbitrage business, and he lived it in 99 when bandwidth was $1,500/megabit and the only way to get it was a 3 year contract. By 2001 it was $50 - If you were holding that on borrowed money you were dead. His case for $CRWV being different is that AI compute is in a massive shortage, so GPU and data center prices keep rising. Maybe he's right. But the neocloud model is still a levered bet that GPU scarcity outlasts the debt, because they borrow against the GPUs and the lenders get paid on a schedule whether or not the market cooperates. A compute subnet on Bittensor is basically a decentralized neocloud that doesn't need any of that. There's no GPU purchase to finance (miners show up with their own hardware) and no 3 year capacity contract to get stuck holding if prices move. The token + the network do the job the debt does for CoreWeave. Emissions bootstrap the supply side, and as demand and revenue grow the subnet puts that value back into its token, which raises what miners earn and pulls more compute onto the network. The token is the lever that scales how much compute you can harvest and coordinate. So if GPU pricing ever pulls a Loudcloud, the subnet doesn't blow up, its incentives just buy more compute than they used to. With no debt there's nothing to default on, and nobody can call a loan or force a fire sale. The risk you take on instead is token volatility, which you manage with a treasury (keep cash on hand and use it to support your token through drawdowns). A bad market can starve a subnet for a while, but one with real demand underneath it can ride that out. The tradeoff is a slower, more gradual build. A neocloud can borrow its way to a giant cluster fast, while a subnet's capacity grows with the size of the network and the token. What you get in exchange is a far more durable business, mostly because of where the supply comes from. You're tapping a bunch of long tails of compute that a neocloud can't really get at: >people who own their own hardware and want to monetize it when they're not using it >slack capacity in data centers (nobody runs at 100%), which can get sold into the subnet's spot market instead of sitting idle >sunk cost hardware, i.e. paid off GPUs that can't get a contract for anything else >operators in places with cheap power that no lender would ever underwrite a data center for Once a card is paid off the main ongoing cost is power, which even on an H100 is something like 5-10 cents an hour depending on where you are. So a lot of this supply is pretty price insensitive. They make more when the token is higher, but a 50% drawdown in miner rewards eats into their margin and plenty of them keep mining anyway. That gives you a structural supply floor that doesn't really care what the token (and therefore the miner reward) is doing day to day. Then as network value and the token go up, you progressively unlock compute that's more price sensitive (financed GPUs that still have to pay themselves off, US data centers with pricier power, etc). Each one joins once mining becomes economic for it, and you get a flywheel: token up → more of the world's compute profitable to plug in → more capacity to sell → more revenue → more value back into the token → repeat. Every GPU that joins also makes the network cheaper and more reliable to buy from, so you get a real network effect on top of removing the debt risk. And in the limit it can reach more compute than any single hyperscaler could ever build or finance, because the supply side is permissionless and global. You start by tapping into the world's edge compute, and over time the rest of the world's compute comes online as it makes economic sense for whoever owns it.

The only way to combat a threat like this is to welcome it and learn from it. By constantly ingesting and evolving attack vectors from a hive mind of miners, a Bittensor powered defence has now become the only reliable source of protection on the internet.

title: RT by @PanteraCapital: In 2024, an employee at engineering firm Arup transferred $25.6 million after joining a video call where every other participant was a deepfake. Since then, AI has advanced significantly and is making impersonation increasingly convincing, causing challenges for financial institutions in particular. As autonomous agents begin handling more financial activity on behalf of people, establishing an added layer of trust and security behind a transaction or sensitive conversation is becoming an urgent need. Introducing @world_id for banking and finance, a suite of technologies that helps institutions establish trust through privacy-preserving cryptographic Proofs. World ID for Zoom lets meeting participants confirm they are the same Orb-verified human connected to their account, while World ID for agents allows AI agents to carry Proofs delegated by people. Bain Capital, OpenExchange, Outtake, Pantera Capital, and VanEck Funds are initial design partners, bringing World ID into some of finance's most consequential interactions. https://fortune.com/2026/10/18/zoom-adds-proof-of-human-feature-to-stop-deep-fakes-toowith-tech/

title: The future of cybersecurity will be dictated by a defender's ability to not only ingest unique attacks, but generate the strains that don't exist yet and ship the detection ahead of them. As the rest of the industry degrades, the largest financial institutions will consolidate on the single provider that can do this at scale. That provider needs a constant supply of unique attacks to work from, and a subnet is the only structure that pays a swarm of attackers to supply them. bittensor:native #SN61
